raw:
“I’ll see you tomorrow,” you tell Owen.

He pauses with his mug halfway to the table.

“I’m not in tomorrow. That’s the shift I moved. Friday.”

He does not press for an answer about the archive. When his break ends, he returns to the carton of lanyards.

You step out onto Harbour Street alone and walk downhill towards the water. The rain has passed, leaving the paving dark between the buildings. A cold breeze comes through the harbour mouth and moves the hem of your charcoal coat.

Along the inner quay, two fishing boats sit against rubber fenders while their crews unload grey crates onto a trolley. Diesel hangs in the air with salt, wet rope and the sharper smell from a bin of old bait. Farther along, somebody runs a pressure hose across a deck; water rattles over the stone edge and falls into the harbour.

You follow the quay past stacked lobster pots and a row of iron bollards rubbed bright at their tops. The tide is low enough to expose weed on the lower steps. Gulls pick through the shallows without coming near you.

No one stops you. At the end of the inner harbour, you turn back by the same route. The walk uses the rest of your break, and you reach the Picture House before your archive work is due to resume.
